Reference: Desmet, Nagy and Rossi-Hansberg (2018); Link 1; Link 2

Model Setting

The paper asks how the world's economic geography shapes long-run development and how much migration restrictions cost. It builds a dynamic spatial growth model with realistic geography: a continuum of locations that differ in amenities, productivity, land and position, costly trade in the manner of Eaton and Kortum (2002), costly migration with heterogeneous location tastes, local innovation whose payoff depends on market size, and slow spatial diffusion of technology. Two assumptions keep the dynamics tractable. Migration costs are the product of an origin and a destination component, which makes the location choice static, and firms compete for land, which drives profits to zero in every period and makes the innovation choice static. The equilibrium therefore reduces, period by period, to a system of integral equations in utility, population density and wages, for which the authors prove existence and uniqueness with the results of Zabreyko et al. (1975), first used in spatial models by Allen and Arkolakis (2014). The same structure gives a parameter condition under which a unique balanced-growth path (BGP) exists, with a growth rate that depends on the world distribution of population.

The model is taken to the whole world at a resolution of one degree by one degree (64,800 grid cells) with a period of one year and the year 2000 as period 0. Data on land, population and income per capita are inverted to recover amenities relative to utility and initial productivity, subjective well-being from the Gallup World Poll pins down initial utility, and population changes between 2000 and 2005 identify migration costs. With current migration frictions the economy takes about 400 years to reach its BGP, world real output growth rises from 2 percent to about 2.9 percent by 2100 and settles slightly above 2.8 percent, and the correlation between population density and real income per capita across cells rises from −0.41-0.41−0.41 today to about 0.65: today's dense and poor regions in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and East Asia become the productive regions of the future (a productivity reversal). Fully liberalizing migration moves 70.3 percent of the world population across countries at impact and raises the present discounted value of real output by 126 percent and of welfare by 306 percent.

Migration Costs and Location Choice

The key assumption on migration costs is that they decompose into an origin and a destination component and that staying is free:

m(s,r)=m1(s)m2(r),m(r,r)=1⇒m1(r)=1m2(r)(4)m(s,r)=m_1(s)m_2(r),\qquad m(r,r)=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad m_1(r)=\frac{1}{m_2(r)} \tag{4}m(s,r)=m1​(s)m2​(r),m(r,r)=1⇒m1​(r)=m2​(r)1​(4)

A migrant who enters rrr pays the flow cost m2(r)m_2(r)m2​(r) for as long as she stays there, and receives it back as the benefit m1(r)m_1(r)m1​(r) on leaving. The product of all past moving costs therefore telescopes to m1(r0)m2(rt)m_1(r_0)m_2(r_t)m1​(r0​)m2​(rt​), and log flow utility depends only on the initial location (which is not a choice) and the current one:

ln⁡uti(r0,rt)=ln⁡ut(rt)−ln⁡m1(r0)−ln⁡m2(rt)+ln⁡εti(rt)(5)\ln u^i_t(r_0,r_t)=\ln u_t(r_t)-\ln m_1(r_0)-\ln m_2(r_t)+\ln\varepsilon^i_t(r_t) \tag{5}lnuti​(r0​,rt​)=lnut​(rt​)−lnm1​(r0​)−lnm2​(rt​)+lnεti​(rt​)(5)

The location decision is static: it is independent of the agent's history and of the future path of the economy, and the model only needs to track net population by location. With Frechet shocks, the fraction of the population of sss that chooses rrr is the same for every origin:

Firm Problem and Land Competition

Profits are linear in land, so in any small interval a continuum of firms compete in prices. Spatial correlation of the draws and continuity of amenities and transport costs make their costs arbitrarily similar as the interval shrinks, which yields perfect local competition. After observing the common local draw, a potential firm at rrr maximizes current profits per unit of land:

Firms bid for land up to the point of zero profits after covering the innovation cost wt(r)νϕtω(r)ξw_t(r)\nu\phi^\omega_t(r)^{\xi}wt​(r)νϕtω​(r)ξ. Innovation today raises local productivity tomorrow through the law of motion for τt(r)\tau_t(r)τt​(r), but the innovating firm earns zero profits in every future period whatever it invests, because the gains are bid into land rents and next period's technology is available to all potential entrants at rrr. The dynamic innovation problem is therefore a sequence of static problems: firms innovate to maximize their current bid for land, as in Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg (2014). Under continuity of all primitive functions, the system reduces to three equations in wages, density and utility (Lemma 2). Given τt(⋅)\tau_t(\cdot)τt​(⋅), the schedules wt(⋅)w_t(\cdot)wt​(⋅), Lˉt(⋅)\bar{L}_t(\cdot)Lˉt​(⋅) and ut(⋅)u_t(\cdot)ut​(⋅) satisfy the population equation together with a wage equation:

and an integral equation that combines the price index with trade balance:

where wˉ\bar{w}wˉ and κ1\kappa_1κ1​ are constants. The wage equation follows from the symmetry of trade costs: the origin and destination terms of the gravity system are proportional, as in Allen and Arkolakis (2014). Past decisions enter only through τt(⋅)\tau_t(\cdot)τt​(⋅), and amenities enter only relative to utility, as aˉ(r)/ut(r)\bar{a}(r)/u_t(r)aˉ(r)/ut​(r). A solution exists and is unique, and can be found by iteration, under the following condition (Lemma 3 and Proposition 1):

αθ+γ1ξ≤λ+1−μ+Ω(23)\frac{\alpha}{\theta}+\frac{\gamma_1}{\xi}\leq\lambda+1-\mu+\Omega \tag{23}θα​+ξγ1​​≤λ+1−μ+Ω(23)

The static agglomeration forces, namely the production externality α/θ\alpha/\thetaα/θ and the returns to innovation γ1/ξ\gamma_1/\xiγ1​/ξ, must not dominate the three dispersion forces: congestion in amenities λ\lambdaλ, decreasing returns to labor on fixed land 1−μ1-\mu1−μ, and taste dispersion Ω\OmegaΩ. The proof substitutes the population equation into the integral equation, which already incorporates the wage equation, and applies Theorem 2.19 of Zabreyko et al. (1975), which requires the ratio of the exponents on the two sides of the resulting equation in ut(⋅)u_t(\cdot)ut​(⋅) to be at most one in absolute value. Solving the system period by period and updating τt(⋅)\tau_t(\cdot)τt​(⋅) gives a unique equilibrium path from τ0(⋅)\tau_0(\cdot)τ0​(⋅) and Lˉ0(⋅)\bar{L}_0(\cdot)Lˉ0​(⋅). Lemma 3 as printed states the condition with a strict inequality, whereas the text before it and Proposition 1 use the weak inequality; the strict version is what the iterative procedure needs.

Balanced-Growth Path

In a BGP all locations grow at the same rate, and the distributions of density and innovation, written Lˉ(⋅)\bar{L}(\cdot)Lˉ(⋅) and ϕ(⋅)\phi(\cdot)ϕ(⋅) without time subscripts, are constant. Dividing the law of motion by τt(r)\tau_t(r)τt​(r) shows that the growth rate of technology is ϕt(r)θγ1[∫Sητt(s)/τt(r)ds]1−γ2\phi_t(r)^{\theta\gamma_1}[\int_S\eta\tau_t(s)/\tau_t(r)ds]^{1-\gamma_2}ϕt​(r)θγ1​[∫S​ητt​(s)/τt​(r)ds]1−γ2​. Equating this rate across two locations and using the link between innovation and density gives relative productivities as a function of relative densities:

τt(s)τt(r)=[ϕ(s)ϕ(r)]θγ11−γ2=[Lˉ(s)Lˉ(r)]θγ1[1−γ2]ξ(24)\frac{\tau_t(s)}{\tau_t(r)}=\left[\frac{\phi(s)}{\phi(r)}\right]^{\frac{\theta\gamma_1}{1-\gamma_2}}=\left[\frac{\bar{L}(s)}{\bar{L}(r)}\right]^{\frac{\theta\gamma_1}{[1-\gamma_2]\xi}} \tag{24}τt​(r)τt​(s)​=[ϕ(r)ϕ(s)​]1−γ2​θγ1​​=[Lˉ(r)Lˉ(s)​][1−γ2​]ξθγ1​​(24)

Substituting into the equilibrium system gives an equation for the BGP distribution of utility, which has a unique positive solution if (Lemma 4):

αθ+γ1ξ+γ1[1−γ2]ξ≤λ+1−μ+Ω(25)\frac{\alpha}{\theta}+\frac{\gamma_1}{\xi}+\frac{\gamma_1}{[1-\gamma_2]\xi}\leq\lambda+1-\mu+\Omega \tag{25}θα​+ξγ1​​+[1−γ2​]ξγ1​​≤λ+1−μ+Ω(25)

The extra term on the left is the dynamic agglomeration effect: denser places innovate more and so become more productive over time, and diffusion is what keeps this effect bounded. Without diffusion (γ2=1\gamma_2=1γ2​=1) the condition never holds and there is no BGP with a non-degenerate distribution of employment. The condition is strictly stronger than the one for equilibrium: an equilibrium can exist when it fails, but activity may then concentrate progressively in an area of measure zero. (The paper refers here to the condition in Lemma 1, but the equilibrium condition is the one in Lemma 3.) In the BGP ut+1(r)/ut(r)=[τt+1(r)/τt(r)]1/θu_{t+1}(r)/u_t(r)=[\tau_{t+1}(r)/\tau_t(r)]^{1/\theta}ut+1​(r)/ut​(r)=[τt+1​(r)/τt​(r)]1/θ, and welfare and real consumption grow everywhere at the rate (Lemma 5):

ut+1(r)ut(r)=η1−γ2θ[γ1/νγ1+μξ]γ1ξ[∫SLˉ(s)θγ1[1−γ2]ξds]1−γ2θ(26)\frac{u_{t+1}(r)}{u_t(r)}=\eta^{\frac{1-\gamma_2}{\theta}}\left[\frac{\gamma_1/\nu}{\gamma_1+\mu\xi}\right]^{\frac{\gamma_1}{\xi}}\left[\int_S\bar{L}(s)^{\frac{\theta\gamma_1}{[1-\gamma_2]\xi}}ds\right]^{\frac{1-\gamma_2}{\theta}} \tag{26}ut​(r)ut+1​(r)​=ηθ1−γ2​​[γ1​+μξγ1​/ν​]ξγ1​​[∫S​Lˉ(s)[1−γ2​]ξθγ1​​ds]θ1−γ2​​(26)

Growth depends on the size of world population and on its distribution in space. When the exponent θγ1/([1−γ2]ξ)\theta\gamma_1/([1-\gamma_2]\xi)θγ1​/([1−γ2​]ξ) exceeds one, a more concentrated population raises growth. The formula has a strong scale effect in total population, which the authors note could be removed by making the innovation cost increase with world population.

Calibration

Table 1 of the paper assigns the parameters as follows.

  • Preferences: β=0.965\beta=0.965β=0.965 (annual; it must discount faster than the BGP growth rate, which never exceeds 3.5 percent in the benchmark and the migration counterfactuals). ρ=0.75\rho=0.75ρ=0.75, an elasticity of substitution of 4 (Bernard et al. 2003). Ω=0.5\Omega=0.5Ω=0.5: by the migration share equation, 1/Ω1/\Omega1/Ω is the elasticity of migration flows to real income, set to 2 from studies of settings without formal restrictions (intra-EU and intra-US migration, for example Monte, Redding and Rossi-Hansberg 2018).

  • Amenity congestion: λ=0.32\lambda=0.32λ=0.32, from a two-stage least squares regression of log amenities on log population for 192 US metropolitan areas (data of Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg 2013), with exogenous productivity as the instrument for population.

  • Technology: θ=6.5\theta=6.5θ=6.5, between the 8.3 of Eaton and Kortum (2002) and the 4.6 of Simonovska and Waugh (2014). μ=0.8\mu=0.8μ=0.8, a non-land share (land including structures has a share of about 0.2). α=0.06\alpha=0.06α=0.06, so the static agglomeration elasticity is α/θ≈0.01\alpha/\theta\approx0.01α/θ≈0.01, slightly below Carlino, Chatterjee and Hunt (2007) because the model also has dynamic agglomeration. ξ=125\xi=125ξ=125 from Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg (2015). ν=0.15\nu=0.15ν=0.15 matches an initial world growth rate of real GDP of 2 percent.

  • Innovation and diffusion: γ1=0.319\gamma_1=0.319γ1​=0.319 and γ2=0.993\gamma_2=0.993γ2​=0.993, from the relation between growth and the spatial distribution of population described below.

  • Trade costs: per-cell passing costs from Allen and Arkolakis (2014) and the exponent Υ=0.393\Upsilon=0.393Υ=0.393, described below.

With these values the left-hand side of the BGP condition is about 0.38 and the right-hand side is 1.02, so the equilibrium is unique and converges to a unique BGP. To identify γ1\gamma_1γ1​ and γ2\gamma_2γ2​, the authors assume that each country ccc is on a BGP with its own growth rate and take logs of the growth formula on a grid of cells:

log⁡yt+1(c)−log⁡yt(c)=α1+α2log⁡∑ScLc(s)α3,α2=[1−γ2]θ,α3=θγ1[1−γ2]ξ(27)\log y_{t+1}(c)-\log y_t(c)=\alpha_1+\alpha_2\log\sum_{S_c}L_c(s)^{\alpha_3},\qquad\alpha_2=\frac{[1-\gamma_2]}{\theta},\quad\alpha_3=\frac{\theta\gamma_1}{[1-\gamma_2]\xi} \tag{27}logyt+1​(c)−logyt​(c)=α1​+α2​logSc​∑​Lc​(s)α3​,α2​=θ[1−γ2​]​,α3​=[1−γ2​]ξθγ1​​(27)

where the sum is over the cells of country ccc and is divided by the number of cells before estimation. Using G-Econ 4.0 data for 1990, 1995, 2000 and 2005 (106 countries with at least 20 cells) and the between estimator, they obtain α2=0.00116\alpha_2=0.00116α2​=0.00116 and α3=2.2\alpha_3=2.2α3​=2.2, which give the values above given θ\thetaθ and ξ\xiξ. Transport costs are built from geography. The cost of passing through cell rrr, ς(r)\varsigma(r)ς(r), is log-linear in the shares of the cell with rail, major roads, other roads and water access, with coefficients ςrail=0.1434\varsigma_{\text{rail}}=0.1434ςrail​=0.1434, ςno_rail=0.4302\varsigma_{\text{no\_rail}}=0.4302ςno_rail​=0.4302, ςmajor_road=0.5636\varsigma_{\text{major\_road}}=0.5636ςmajor_road​=0.5636, ςother_road=1.1272\varsigma_{\text{other\_road}}=1.1272ςother_road​=1.1272, ςno_road=1.9726\varsigma_{\text{no\_road}}=1.9726ςno_road​=1.9726 and ςwater=0.0779\varsigma_{\text{water}}=0.0779ςwater​=0.0779 (the published Table 1 prints 0.0779 for ςno_water\varsigma_{\text{no\_water}}ςno_water​ as well, a misprint that would make water access irrelevant; the same calibration in Desmet et al. (2021) lists ςno_water=0.779\varsigma_{\text{no\_water}}=0.779ςno_water​=0.779). The fast marching algorithm then finds the least-cost path g(r,s)g(r,s)g(r,s) between any two cells on the sphere:

ς(r,s)=[inf⁡g(r,s)∫g(r,s)ς(u)du]Υ(28)\varsigma(r,s)=\left[\inf_{g(r,s)}\int_{g(r,s)}\varsigma(u)du\right]^{\Upsilon} \tag{28}ς(r,s)=[g(r,s)inf​∫g(r,s)​ς(u)du]Υ(28)

The exponent Υ\UpsilonΥ is chosen so that a gravity regression on trade flows simulated for the initial period reproduces a distance elasticity of −0.93-0.93−0.93 (Head and Mayer 2014). The implied within-country elasticity is −1.32-1.32−1.32, and the model's untargeted world trade share of 14.1 percent of GDP in 2000 matches the data.

Model Inversion

The fundamentals aˉ(r)\bar{a}(r)aˉ(r) and τ0(r)\tau_0(r)τ0​(r) are recovered from data on land H(r)H(r)H(r), population density Lˉ0(r)\bar{L}_0(r)Lˉ0​(r) and wages w0(r)w_0(r)w0​(r), measured by GDP per capita in 2000 (G-Econ 4.0). Inverting the wage equation at t=0t=0t=0 gives initial productivity:

τ0(r)=wˉ−(1+2θ)[aˉ(r)u0(r)]θH(r)w0(r)1+2θLˉ0(r)1−α−[λ+γ1ξ−[1−μ]]θ(29)\tau_0(r)=\bar{w}^{-(1+2\theta)}\left[\frac{\bar{a}(r)}{u_0(r)}\right]^{\theta}H(r)w_0(r)^{1+2\theta}\bar{L}_0(r)^{1-\alpha-\left[\lambda+\frac{\gamma_1}{\xi}-[1-\mu]\right]\theta} \tag{29}τ0​(r)=wˉ−(1+2θ)[u0​(r)aˉ(r)​]θH(r)w0​(r)1+2θLˉ0​(r)1−α−[λ+ξγ1​​−[1−μ]]θ(29)

and substituting it into the integral equation leaves one equation in the amenity-to-utility ratio:

w0(r)−θLˉ0(r)λθ[aˉ(r)u0(r)]−θ=κ1wˉ−(1+2θ)∫Sw0(s)1+θLˉ0(s)1−λθH(s)ς(r,s)−θ[aˉ(s)u0(s)]θds(30)w_0(r)^{-\theta}\bar{L}_0(r)^{\lambda\theta}\left[\frac{\bar{a}(r)}{u_0(r)}\right]^{-\theta}=\kappa_1\bar{w}^{-(1+2\theta)}\int_Sw_0(s)^{1+\theta}\bar{L}_0(s)^{1-\lambda\theta}H(s)\varsigma(r,s)^{-\theta}\left[\frac{\bar{a}(s)}{u_0(s)}\right]^{\theta}ds \tag{30}w0​(r)−θLˉ0​(r)λθ[u0​(r)aˉ(r)​]−θ=κ1​wˉ−(1+2θ)∫S​w0​(s)1+θLˉ0​(s)1−λθH(s)ς(r,s)−θ[u0​(s)aˉ(s)​]θds(30)

The solution for aˉ(r)/u0(r)\bar{a}(r)/u_0(r)aˉ(r)/u0​(r), and hence for τ0(r)\tau_0(r)τ0​(r), exists and is unique (Lemma 6), with wˉ\bar{w}wˉ normalized to the world average wage in 2000. Population and income alone identify only the ratio. A poor and dense place such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo has a high ratio, which under free mobility would have to be read as excellent amenities, and which with migration frictions can instead reflect low utility of people who are trapped there. To separate the two, the paper uses the Cantril ladder of subjective well-being from the Gallup World Poll, a score from 0 to 10. Deaton and Stone (2013) find that the ladder is linear in the log of real income with a slope of about 0.55, whereas model utility is linear in the level of real income, so the ladder score uˇ\check{u}uˇ is converted to a cardinal utility level by:

u0(r)=eψuˇ(c(r)),ψ=1.8(31)u_0(r)=e^{\psi\check{u}(c(r))},\qquad\psi=1.8 \tag{31}u0​(r)=eψuˇ(c(r)),ψ=1.8(31)

where uˇ(c(r))\check{u}(c(r))uˇ(c(r)) is the average ladder score of the country to which rrr belongs and ψ\psiψ is the inverse of the slope. Initial utility therefore varies only across countries, and aˉ(r)\bar{a}(r)aˉ(r) follows from the ratio. The recovered amenities correlate as expected with distance to water, elevation, precipitation, temperature and vegetation, across the world, within the United States and across countries, while placebo amenities built by assuming equal utility in all countries do not. Entry migration costs are identified from the population distribution in period 1, taken from 2005 data with the five-year change divided by five. The population equation gives period-1 utility as a function of population and the entry cost:

u1(r)=H(r)ΩLˉ1(r)Ωm^2(r),m^2(r)=m2(r)LˉΩ[∫Su1(v)1/Ωm2(v)−1/Ωdv]−Ω(32)u_1(r)=H(r)^{\Omega}\bar{L}_1(r)^{\Omega}\hat{m}_2(r),\qquad\hat{m}_2(r)=\frac{m_2(r)}{\bar{L}^{\Omega}\left[\int_Su_1(v)^{1/\Omega}m_2(v)^{-1/\Omega}dv\right]^{-\Omega}} \tag{32}u1​(r)=H(r)ΩLˉ1​(r)Ωm^2​(r),m^2​(r)=LˉΩ[∫S​u1​(v)1/Ωm2​(v)−1/Ωdv]−Ωm2​(r)​(32)

Substituting this into the integral equation for period 1, with τ1(⋅)\tau_1(\cdot)τ1​(⋅) computed from τ0(⋅)\tau_0(\cdot)τ0​(⋅) and Lˉ0(⋅)\bar{L}_0(\cdot)Lˉ0​(⋅) through the law of motion, gives an equation in aˉ(r)/m^2(r)\bar{a}(r)/\hat{m}_2(r)aˉ(r)/m^2​(r) whose solution exists, is unique and can be found by iteration (Lemma 7), because the ratio of the exponents on its two sides is θ/(1+θ)<1\theta/(1+\theta)<1θ/(1+θ)<1. The costs m2(⋅)m_2(\cdot)m2​(⋅) are identified up to scale and normalized so that their minimum is one, so entering any location is weakly costly. They make the model match observed population changes exactly and capture all barriers, legal, informational and psychological. Entry is very costly into Scandinavia, parts of Canada and the United States, Australia and New Zealand, and cheap into Africa, India and China.

Simulation and Backcasting

Given the parameters and aˉ(⋅)\bar{a}(\cdot)aˉ(⋅), τ0(⋅)\tau_0(\cdot)τ0​(⋅), m2(⋅)m_2(\cdot)m2​(⋅) and ς(⋅,⋅)\varsigma(\cdot,\cdot)ς(⋅,⋅), the model is simulated forward by solving the three-equation system in each period and updating productivity. Counterfactual migration regimes replace the entry cost with m2(⋅)ϑm_2(\cdot)^{\vartheta}m2​(⋅)ϑ for ϑ∈[0,1]\vartheta\in[0,1]ϑ∈[0,1]: ϑ=1\vartheta=1ϑ=1 keeps the estimated frictions and ϑ=0\vartheta=0ϑ=0 is free mobility, with m(s,r)=1m(s,r)=1m(s,r)=1 for all pairs. Average productivity in a cell is measured as [τt(r)Lˉt(r)α]1/θ[\tau_t(r)\bar{L}_t(r)^{\alpha}]^{1/\theta}[τt​(r)Lˉt​(r)α]1/θ, and world aggregates are population-weighted averages. The system can also be solved backward, obtaining Lˉt(⋅)\bar{L}_t(\cdot)Lˉt​(⋅) and τt(⋅)\tau_t(\cdot)τt​(⋅) from τt+1(⋅)\tau_{t+1}(\cdot)τt+1​(⋅), under a condition that is weaker than the one for equilibrium because dynamic agglomeration is not an issue when time runs backward. Running the model back from 2000 to 1870 serves as an over-identification test. Country-level correlations between model and data for log population exceed 0.96 back to 1950 and are 0.68 for 1870, and the correlation of population growth between year ttt and 2000 is 0.74 for 1950 and 0.34 for 1870.

Counterfactual Results

Welfare is the present discounted value of the population-weighted average of ut(r)u_t(r)ut​(r), or alternatively of the expected utility including taste shocks. Changes are relative to ϑ=1\vartheta=1ϑ=1.

  • Current frictions (ϑ=1\vartheta=1ϑ=1): about 0.3 percent of the world population moves across countries per year and 0.45 percent across cells, and the flows vanish in the BGP, which is reached after about 400 years. Real GDP growth rises from 2 percent to about 2.9 percent and ends slightly above 2.8 percent, and utility growth rises from about 2.4 to 2.8 percent. The correlation between density and productivity across cells rises from about 0.38 to 1.0 by period 600, while that between density and real income per capita never exceeds 0.7. High density in today's poor countries means high future innovation there, so sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and East Asia become dense, productive and congested, and North America and Europe fall behind in population and productivity, though not in ut(r)u_t(r)ut​(r). The world trade share rises from 14.1 to 15.1 percent by 2600.

  • Free mobility (ϑ=0\vartheta=0ϑ=0): 70.3 percent of the population changes country at impact (71.6 percent changes cell). The present discounted value of real income rises by 125.8 percent and of welfare by 305.9 percent, or by 79.0 percent when welfare includes taste shocks, since residents are less selected when moving is free. The initial correlation of density and productivity jumps from 0.38 to 0.69, no productivity reversal occurs, and Europe and the eastern United States remain strong while high-amenity places such as parts of Brazil, Mexico and Venezuela become dense and productive. BGP growth of real GDP is about 0.5 percentage points higher. Utility growth falls in the short run because of congestion in destinations and rises strongly after about 2200. Nearly 60 percent of the welfare gain comes from relocating people to high-amenity places, so liberalization makes the future high-productivity regions coincide with the high-amenity ones.

  • Partial liberalization: gains are monotone in the degree of liberalization. For ϑ=0.75\vartheta=0.75ϑ=0.75, 21.2 percent of the population moves at impact, real income rises by 30.6 percent and welfare by 59.8 percent (19.2 percent with taste shocks). For ϑ=0.5\vartheta=0.5ϑ=0.5 the figures are 43.2, 69.2 and 144.3 percent (40.5), and for ϑ=0.375\vartheta=0.375ϑ=0.375 they are 52.7, 87.1 and 188.8 percent (50.3).

  • Trade and migration: raising trade costs by 40 percent lowers real income by 30.1 percent and welfare by 34.2 percent, an order of magnitude more than in static one-sector models (2.28 percent in Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare 2014), and cuts the trade share to 3.9 percent. With these higher trade costs, free migration raises real income by 156.9 percent and welfare by 382.9 percent, so trade and migration are substitutes.

  • Robustness: with Ω=0.6\Omega=0.6Ω=0.6 the welfare gain from free mobility is 243.0 percent. With amenity congestion lowered to λ=0.256\lambda=0.256λ=0.256 it is 549.1 percent, and the real income gain is 174.0 percent. A 20 percent higher α\alphaα changes little (126.6 and 309.4 percent). Technology diffusion that decays with distance gives a real income gain of 131.8 percent and a welfare gain of 224.9 percent.

This is the primitive period utility. It multiplies four objects: the local amenity at(r)a_t(r)at​(r), a CES aggregate of the consumption of the continuum of goods ω∈[0,1]\omega\in[0,1]ω∈[0,1], the idiosyncratic taste shock εti(r)\varepsilon^i_t(r)εti​(r), and the inverse of the product of all moving costs the agent has ever paid, ∏s=1tm(rs−1,rs)−1\prod_{s=1}^{t}m(r_{s-1},r_s)^{-1}∏s=1t​m(rs−1​,rs​)−1. With 0<ρ<10<\rho<10<ρ<1 the goods are imperfect substitutes with elasticity 1/(1−ρ)1/(1-\rho)1/(1−ρ), which is 4 at the calibrated ρ=0.75\rho=0.75ρ=0.75.

The multiplicative form is what makes the model tractable. Because the CES aggregate is homogeneous of degree one, the consumption term equals real income, so utility is amenity times real income times taste, as in equation (3). Because migration costs enter as a permanent flow cost rather than a one-off payment, an agent who moved many times carries the whole product of past costs for ever; combined with the decomposition in equation (4) this product telescopes, which is the step that turns the location choice into a static problem in equation (5).

A simple illustration: an agent who never moves has rs=r0r_s=r_0rs​=r0​ for all sss, every factor is m(r0,r0)=1m(r_0,r_0)=1m(r0​,r0​)=1, and her utility is

uti=at(r0)[∫01ctω(r0)ρdω]1/ρεti(r0).u^i_t=a_t(r_0)\left[\int_0^1c^\omega_t(r_0)^{\rho}d\omega\right]^{1/\rho}\varepsilon^i_t(r_0).uti​=at​(r0​)[∫01​ctω​(r0​)ρdω]1/ρεti​(r0​).

Utility is cardinal here: lifetime welfare is ∑tβtuti\sum_t\beta^tu^i_t∑t​βtuti​, linear in the level of utiu^i_tuti​, which matters for the conversion of subjective well-being into utility in equation (31).

The first part specifies amenities as a fundamental component aˉ(r)\bar{a}(r)aˉ(r) scaled down by local density: λ≥0\lambda\geq0λ≥0 is the elasticity of amenities with respect to population per unit of land, a congestion force. Doubling density lowers amenities by the factor 2−λ2^{-\lambda}2−λ, about 20 percent at the calibrated λ=0.32\lambda=0.32λ=0.32. The congestion term is one of the three dispersion forces on the right-hand side of the uniqueness conditions in equations (23) and (25).

The second part says the taste shock is Frechet with unit scale and shape 1/Ω1/\Omega1/Ω. A larger Ω\OmegaΩ means a fatter tail, so tastes are more dispersed and people respond less to differences in ut(r)u_t(r)ut​(r). The Frechet form is chosen because the maximum of independent Frechet variables is again Frechet, which gives the closed-form location shares of equation (6) with migration elasticity 1/Ω1/\Omega1/Ω and the closed-form expected utility of equation (8). The restriction Ω<1\Omega<1Ω<1 is needed for the mean of the shock to be finite:

E[εti(r)]=Γ(1−Ω).E\left[\varepsilon^i_t(r)\right]=\Gamma(1-\Omega).E[εti​(r)]=Γ(1−Ω).

As Ω→0\Omega\to0Ω→0 the distribution collapses to a point mass at one, everyone agrees on the ranking of locations, and the population elasticity 1/Ω1/\Omega1/Ω becomes infinite; this is the free-mobility, equal-utility limit of standard spatial models. With Ω=0.5\Omega=0.5Ω=0.5 the elasticity of population to ut(r)u_t(r)ut​(r) is 2.

The first expression defines real income per capita. Nominal income of a resident of rrr is the wage wt(r)w_t(r)wt​(r) plus an equal share of local land rents: Rt(r)R_t(r)Rt​(r) is rent per unit of land and Lˉt(r)\bar{L}_t(r)Lˉt​(r) is residents per unit of land, so Rt(r)/Lˉt(r)R_t(r)/\bar{L}_t(r)Rt​(r)/Lˉt​(r) is rent per resident. Dividing by the ideal price index Pt(r)P_t(r)Pt​(r) of the CES aggregator converts income into units of the consumption bundle. There is no saving, so consumption equals income.

The second expression defines the deterministic part of utility. Since the CES aggregate in equation (1) is homogeneous of degree one, an agent who spends her income optimally obtains exactly yt(r)y_t(r)yt​(r) from it, and equation (1) becomes

uti(rˉ−,r)=ut(r) εti(r)∏s=1tm(rs−1,rs)−1,ut(r)=at(r)yt(r).u^i_t(\bar{r}_-,r)=u_t(r)\,\varepsilon^i_t(r)\prod_{s=1}^{t}m(r_{s-1},r_s)^{-1},\qquad u_t(r)=a_t(r)y_t(r).uti​(rˉ−​,r)=ut​(r)εti​(r)s=1∏t​m(rs−1​,rs​)−1,ut​(r)=at​(r)yt​(r).

The assumption that rents are rebated locally and equally (rather than to absentee landlords or to a world portfolio) keeps income proportional to the wage: by equation (15) rents are a constant fraction of the wage bill, so yt(r)y_t(r)yt​(r) is the real wage times the constant ξ/(μξ+γ1)\xi/(\mu\xi+\gamma_1)ξ/(μξ+γ1​), which is how equation (20) is obtained. The object ut(r)u_t(r)ut​(r) is what migration responds to in equations (6) and (7), and its population-weighted present value is the main welfare measure.

The first equality is an assumption (Assumption 1 of the paper): the cost of moving from sss to rrr is the product of an origin term and a destination term. The implication follows by evaluating the assumption at s=rs=rs=r and using the second assumption that staying is free:

1=m(r,r)=m1(r)m2(r)⟹m1(r)=1m2(r).1=m(r,r)=m_1(r)m_2(r)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_1(r)=\frac{1}{m_2(r)}.1=m(r,r)=m1​(r)m2​(r)⟹m1​(r)=m2​(r)1​.

So the two components are not independent objects: one function, m2(⋅)m_2(\cdot)m2​(⋅), describes all bilateral costs,

m(s,r)=m2(r)m2(s).m(s,r)=\frac{m_2(r)}{m_2(s)}.m(s,r)=m2​(s)m2​(r)​.

A place that is costly to enter (m2(r)>1m_2(r)>1m2​(r)>1) is equally beneficial to leave. The consequence used in equation (5) is that the product of costs along any history telescopes,

∏s=1tm(rs−1,rs)=∏s=1tm2(rs)m2(rs−1)=m2(rt)m2(r0)=m1(r0)m2(rt).\prod_{s=1}^{t}m(r_{s-1},r_s)=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\frac{m_2(r_s)}{m_2(r_{s-1})}=\frac{m_2(r_t)}{m_2(r_0)}=m_1(r_0)m_2(r_t).s=1∏t​m(rs−1​,rs​)=s=1∏t​m2​(rs−1​)m2​(rs​)​=m2​(r0​)m2​(rt​)​=m1​(r0​)m2​(rt​).

The restriction rules out costs that depend on the pair beyond these two terms (for example on bilateral distance), and it implies m(s,r)m(r,s)=1m(s,r)m(r,s)=1m(s,r)m(r,s)=1: a return trip is free.

Start from equation (1) written with the deterministic utility of equation (3),

This is the production function per unit of land. Output of good ω\omegaω is Cobb-Douglas in production labor per unit of land, Ltω(r)L^\omega_t(r)Ltω​(r), with exponent μ\muμ; land is the implicit second factor with share 1−μ1-\mu1−μ (one unit of land is used, so it does not appear). Two productivity terms multiply labor: the exogenous draw ztω(r)z^\omega_t(r)ztω​(r), and the firm's own innovation ϕtω(r)\phi^\omega_t(r)ϕtω​(r) raised to γ1\gamma_1γ1​.

Because μ<1\mu<1μ<1 at the calibrated value 0.80.80.8, there are decreasing returns to labor on a fixed plot. This is a dispersion force, the term 1−μ1-\mu1−μ in equations (23) and (25). The elasticity γ1\gamma_1γ1​ measures how much a given innovation raises current output; innovation is paid for in labor, νϕtω(r)ξ\nu\phi^\omega_t(r)^{\xi}νϕtω​(r)ξ workers per unit of land, and the assumption ξ>γ1/[1−μ]\xi>\gamma_1/[1-\mu]ξ>γ1​/[1−μ] guarantees that the firm problem in equation (12) is concave and that the bid rent in equation (15) is positive.

Total factor requirements are therefore

Lˉtω(r)=Ltω(r)+νϕtω(r)ξ\bar{L}^\omega_t(r)=L^\omega_t(r)+\nu\phi^\omega_t(r)^{\xi}Lˉtω​(r)=Ltω​(r)+νϕtω​(r)ξ

workers per unit of land. Since innovation costs are per unit of land while its benefit scales with output per unit of land, denser locations spread the cost over more production and innovate more; equation (14) makes this precise. The same innovation also shifts next period's local technology through equation (11).

The innovation that enters is available to all firms at rrr next period, so innovators cannot appropriate future gains; this is what makes the innovation choice static in equation (12). The problem is static even though innovation raises future technology through equation (11). The reason is land competition: future technology at rrr is available to whoever occupies the land, and any future surplus is bid into rents, so future profits are zero whatever the firm does today. The firm therefore maximizes current profit only.

This defines the bilateral iceberg cost from local geography. Each cell uuu has a cost of being crossed, ς(u)\varsigma(u)ς(u), built from its rail, road and water access. A route g(r,s)g(r,s)g(r,s) is a path on the sphere from rrr to sss; the line integral ∫g(r,s)ς(u)du\int_{g(r,s)}\varsigma(u)du∫g(r,s)​ς(u)du is the cumulated cost along that path; the infimum picks the cheapest route, computed with the fast marching algorithm. The result is raised to the power Υ\UpsilonΥ to give ς(r,s)\varsigma(r,s)ς(r,s).

The construction guarantees symmetry, ς(r,s)=ς(s,r)\varsigma(r,s)=\varsigma(s,r)ς(r,s)=ς(s,r), since a path can be travelled in either direction at the same cost; symmetry is what the wage equation (21) requires. The exponent Υ=0.393<1\Upsilon=0.393<1Υ=0.393<1 makes trade costs concave in the cumulated cost, and it is the single parameter that scales how much geography matters: it is chosen so that a gravity regression on simulated period-0 trade flows gives a distance elasticity of −0.93-0.93−0.93. Since ς(r,s)\varsigma(r,s)ς(r,s) enters trade shares as ς(r,s)−θ\varsigma(r,s)^{-\theta}ς(r,s)−θ in equation (17), the elasticity of trade to cumulated cost is

This maps the Cantril ladder score uˇ\check{u}uˇ, a self-reported number between 0 and 10, into the model's cardinal utility. The need for a transformation comes from a mismatch of functional forms. Deaton and Stone (2013) find that the ladder is linear in log real income, uˇ=ρ0ln⁡y+other terms\check{u}=\rho_0\ln y+\text{other terms}uˇ=ρ0​lny+other terms with slope ρ0≈0.55\rho_0\approx0.55ρ0​≈0.55 (written ρ\rhoρ in the paper, unrelated to the CES parameter). In the model, utility is linear in the level of real income by equation (3), so ln⁡u=ln⁡y+ln⁡a\ln u=\ln y+\ln alnu=lny+lna. Matching the income terms gives

A one-point difference on the ladder therefore corresponds to a utility ratio of e1.8≈6e^{1.8}\approx6e1.8≈6. The score is available only by country, so u0(r)u_0(r)u0​(r) is the same for all cells of a country; within-country variation in the ratio aˉ(r)/u0(r)\bar{a}(r)/u_0(r)aˉ(r)/u0​(r) recovered from equation (30) is thus attributed entirely to amenities.

This step is what separates amenities from utility. The inversion in equations (29) and (30) identifies only the ratio; with u0(r)u_0(r)u0​(r) from the ladder, aˉ(r)=[aˉ(r)/u0(r)]u0(r)\bar{a}(r)=[\bar{a}(r)/u_0(r)]u_0(r)aˉ(r)=[aˉ(r)/u0​(r)]u0​(r). Without it one would have to assume equal utility everywhere, which would read the high density of poor countries as excellent amenities. The value of ψ\psiψ matters for welfare numbers because utility levels differ across countries by large factors.
